### Packages and Data

```{r load-packages, message=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

```

## Data set: college recent grads

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(fivethirtyeight)
college_grad_df <- college_recent_grads
# First look at your data set
glimpse(college_grad_df)
```


# Exercise 1: Exploratory Data Analysis

```{r}
college_grad_df %>% 
  ggplot(mapping=aes(x=median)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2500) 
college_grad_df %>%
  group_by(major_category) %>%
  mutate(
    avg_median = mean(median)
  ) %>%
  select(major_category,avg_median) %>%
  unique() %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_median))
```

Histogram shows positive skew with sharp peak between 30000 and 40000.
Engineering majors have highest average median earnings

# Exercise 2: Exploring relationship

```{r}
#Explanatory: sharewomen, response: median
college_grad_df %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  ggplot(
    mapping = aes(x = sharewomen, y = median)
  ) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm",se=FALSE)
```

Negative correlation observed between share of women and median earnings - correlation is not very strong as points are quite spread out from regression line

# Exercise 3: Fit and interpret a numerical predictor

```{r}
share_fit <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(median ~ sharewomen,data=college_grad_df)
share_fit
augment(share_fit$fit) %>% 
  ggplot(
  mapping = aes(x=.fitted,y=.resid)
) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0)
```

y = 56093 - 30670x
A unit increase in the share of women in a major yields an expected average decrease of 30670 in median earnings. A major with no women is predicted to have median earnings of 56093.
Residuals plot is fairly evenly spread out around 0 without any notable patterns - model is fairly suitable

# Exercise 4: Consider a categorical variable instead 

```{r}
college_grad_engineering <- college_grad_df %>%
  mutate(
    engineering = case_when(
      major_category == "Engineering" ~ "Engineering",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )
      linear_reg() %>%
      set_engine("lm") %>%
      fit(median ~ engineering,data = college_grad_engineering)

```
Intercept: Engineering majors have a predicted median earnings of 57383
Slope: Having a major outside of engineering leads to an expected average decrease of 20702 to median earnings

## Data set: Beauty in the classroom

```{r read-data}
evals<-read.csv("data/evals.csv", row.names=1)
```


# Exercise 1: Exploratory Data Analysis

1.  Visualize the distribution of `score` in the dataframe `evals`.

```{r viz-score}
evals %>%
  ggplot(
    mapping = aes(x=score)
  ) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth=0.1)
```

Distribution negatively skewed - unsurprising as most students are taking a course of their own choice and are thus likely to have a positive bias towards the course

2.  Visualize and describe the relationship between `score` and `bty_avg` using `geom_point()` to represent the data. 

```{r scatterplot}
evals %>%
  ggplot(
    mapping = aes(x=bty_avg,y=score)
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_jitter()
```

geom_jitter() displaces points by a small random value on both axes - original plot was misleading as overplotting of many points was hidden

# Exercise 2: Simple Linear regression with a numerical predictor

1. Fit a linear model called `score_bty_fit` to predict average professor evaluation `score` from average beauty rating (`bty_avg`). Print the regression output using `tidy()`.

```{r fit-score_bty_fit}
score_bty_fit <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(score ~ bty_avg, data = evals)
```

```{r tidy-score_bty_fit}
tidy(score_bty_fit)
```

y = 3.88034 + 0.06664x

2. Plot the data again using `geom_jitter()`, and add the regression line.

```{r viz-score_bty_fit}
evals %>%
  ggplot(
    mapping = aes(x=bty_avg,y=score)
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm",se=FALSE)
```

3. Interpret the slope of the linear model in context of the data.

Each unit increase in average beauty score leads to an expected average increase of 0.06664 in course score

4. Interpret the intercept of the linear model in context of the data. Comment on whether or not the intercept makes sense in this context.

Courses taught by 0/10 chopped munters have a predicted score of 3.88034 - interpretation makes sense as a beauty rating of 0 is possible but just really harsh

5. Determine the $R^2$ of the model and interpret it in the context of the data.

```{r R2}
glance(score_bty_fit)$r.squared
```

Variability of data points is not accounted for particularly well by the model

6. Make a plot of residuals vs. predicted values for the model above.

```{r viz-score_bty_fit-diagnostic}
score_bty_aug <- augment(score_bty_fit$fit)

ggplot(
  score_bty_aug,
  mapping = aes(x=.fitted,y=.resid)
) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0)
```
Model fairly suitable as distribution of residuals shows no discernible pattern and is fairly even around y=0

# Exercise 3: Simple Linear regression with a categorical predictor

0. Look at the variable rank, and determine the frequency of each category level.

```{r}
evals %>% count(rank)
```

1. Fit a new linear model called `score_rank_fit` to predict average professor evaluation `score` based on `rank` of the professor.

```{r fit-score_rank_fit}
# fit model
score_rank_fit <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(score ~ rank,data=evals)
# tidy model output
tidy(score_rank_fit)
```

Intercept: Professors of rank 'teaching' have a predicted score of 4.28431
Slope(s): Professors of rank 'tenure track' have an expected average decrease of 0.012968 
in score compared to those of rank 'teaching'
Professors of rank 'tenured' have an expected average decrease of 0.014518 in score compared to those of rank 'teaching'.
2. Fit a new linear model called `score_gender_fit` to predict average professor evaluation `score` based on `gender` of the professor 

```{r fit-score_gender_fit}
# fit model
score_gender_fit <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(score ~ gender,data=evals)
# tidy model output
tidy(score_gender_fit)
```

```{r score_gender_intercept}
# remove eval = FALSE from the code chunk options
score_gender_intercept <- tidy(score_gender_fit) %>% 
  filter(term == "(Intercept)") %>%
  select(estimate) %>%
  pull()
```

```{r score_gender_slope}
# remove eval = FALSE from the code chunk options
score_gender_slope <- tidy(score_gender_fit) %>% 
  filter(term == "gendermale") %>%
  select(estimate) %>%
  pull()
```

Female professors have a predicted score of `r round(score_gender_intercept,6) and male professors have an expected average increase in score by `r round(score_gender_slope,6)`

# Exercise 4: Multiple linear regression

1. Fit a multiple linear regression model, predicting average professor evaluation `score` based on average beauty rating (`bty_avg`) and `gender.`

```{r fit-score_bty_gender_fit}
# fit model
score_bty_gender_fit <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(score ~ bty_avg + gender, data=evals)
# tidy model output
tidy(score_bty_gender_fit)
```
Intercept: Score for a female 0/10 chopped munter is predicted as 3.74734 
Slope(s): All else held constant, each unit increase in average beauty score leads to an expected average increase in score of 0.07416 
All else held constant, male professors have an expected average 0.17239 higher score than female professors
